## Verdict
- Answer: I cannot give a measured volume of news coverage of election misinformation, because no Prism call was run. I can only offer qualitative, memory-based estimates that coverage peaks around US general elections and is concentrated in US and UK outlets.
- Decision: Treat this as a scoping note. Run the calls in Drill-down before any budget, messaging or monitoring decision.
- Confidence: low - there are no measured counts, and every figure below is labelled (est.) or is absent.
- What would change it: Executing the news.trends, news.compare, news.geography and news.critical calls listed below would replace these estimates with measured values.

## What the data shows
No call was executed, so none of these facets has a measured value:
- **Volume with window:** not measurable here. No article count exists for any window.
- **Monthly series and direction:** not measured. The shape in the Trend section is an illustrative estimate (est.).
- **Tone vs corpus baseline:** cannot be measured. I have no sentiment data and no baseline.
- **Themes:** I cannot give counts. Recurring themes I recall from 2016–2024 coverage are foreign interference, social-platform moderation, "stolen election" claims, voting-machine claims and AI deepfakes (est.).
- **Entities (organisations and people):** I cannot give counts. Entities that routinely appear are Meta, X/Twitter, YouTube, TikTok, CISA and the Election Integrity Partnership (est.).
- **Places and placed_pct:** not measured. I do not know what share of articles could be assigned to a place, so any geographic statement is unverified.
- **Critical headlines with date, publisher and url:** I will not invent any. news.critical (f3) would return them.
- **Source concentration:** not measured. I expect a few large outlets to dominate (est.), but I cannot quantify this.

## Trend
The chart below is a stylised estimate, not data. It uses an index where the US election-year peak is set to 100, and the values are my guesses (est.).

```prism-chart
{"id":"trend-illustrative","kind":"line","title":"Illustrative relative coverage index of election misinformation (peak=100)","unit":"index (est.)","window":{"from":"2024-01-01","to":"2024-12-01"},"x":{"field":"period","type":"temporal"},"series":[{"name":"Relative coverage (illustrative)","source":"estimate","points":[["2024-01",30],["2024-03",35],["2024-06",45],["2024-09",70],["2024-11",100],["2024-12",50]]}],"caption":"Coverage is expected to rise toward election day and fall afterwards; the values are guesses (est.), not measurements.","supports":"Coverage is expected to rise toward election day and fall afterwards."}
```

Coverage is expected to rise toward election day and fall afterwards. The size of the change (the peak is roughly 3x January in this sketch, est.) is not measured. I cannot state the direction for 2025–2026.

## Comparison
I cannot supply a comparison on one scale, because I have no baseline corpus and no measured counts for either side. A valid comparison would define the baseline as all indexed news over the same window, then report election-misinformation articles as a share of it, with the delta and ratio against a prior election cycle. This is specified in f2.

## Geography (optional)
Not measured. I expect the US and UK to dominate, with India, Brazil and EU states following (est.). The placed_pct caveat applies: articles without an identifiable place would be excluded, so any country ranking covers only the placed share.

## Drill-down
Layers to break down: month (period), country (ISO code), outlet (domain), theme, entity.

```prism-calls
[
{"id":"f1","question":"What is the monthly article count for election misinformation over the last 36 months?","feature":"news.trends","args":{"term":"election misinformation","months":36}},
{"id":"f2","question":"How does tone compare with the whole-corpus baseline?","feature":"news.compare","args":{"term":"election misinformation","baseline":"corpus"}},
{"id":"f3","question":"Which critical headlines (date, publisher, url) are most prominent?","feature":"news.critical","args":{"term":"election misinformation","limit":8}},
{"id":"f4","question":"Which countries carry the coverage, and what is placed_pct?","feature":"news.geography","args":{"term":"election misinformation"}},
{"id":"f5","question":"What are the main themes, organisations and people?","feature":"news.overview","args":{"term":"election misinformation"}},
{"id":"f6","question":"How concentrated is coverage across outlets?","feature":"news.overview","args":{"term":"election misinformation","group_by":"source"}},
{"id":"f7","question":"What is the sentiment trend?","feature":"news.sentiment","args":{"term":"election misinformation"}}
]
```

## Exports
```csv name=coverage_template.csv source=estimate window=2024-01-01..2024-12-01 unit=index (est.) coverage=unknown
period,relative_index
2024-01,30
2024-03,35
2024-06,45
2024-09,70
2024-11,100
2024-12,50
```

```json
{"exported_at":"2026-10-23","calls":[]}
```

## Method and limits
- **Windows:** none were queried. The illustrative window ends 2024-12-01, which is about 22 months before today (2026-10-23).
- **Lanes and coverage:** no news or research lane was run, and coverage is unknown.
- **Censoring and match mode:** not applicable, because no search was executed.
- **What the counts are:** the only numbers are illustrative estimates, not article counts and not evidence.
- **Interpretation:** the expected US/UK concentration and the election-peak shape come from memory and are unverified.
- **Cannot answer:** volume, tone versus baseline, placed_pct, headlines and source concentration.

## References
No published references are cited. All figures are labelled (est.).

## Verdict

- Decision: Treat this as a signal to monitor coverage and investigate outlet and geographic patterns, not as a complete census.
- Confidence: medium - the news table passed reachability and historical row-floor checks [c1], but those checks do not prove ingestion completeness; publisher data is a small sample.
- What would change it: A complete, validated article-level dataset with full-window publisher counts and verified relevance.

## What the data shows

The volume is **236 matching articles [c1]**, of which **208 were marked critical [c1]**, in the 24-month window from 2024-06-01 through 2026-06-01 [c1] (end exclusive). These are mention-matched articles, not a count of misinformation incidents, unique claims, or audience exposure. The ingest cutoff is 2026-06-01 [c1]; the latest month is partial and censored, leaving a **five-month gap to today, 2026-10-23 [c1]**.

Tone differs sharply from the corpus baseline: **92.8% negative [c1]** and **6.8% positive [c1]** among matching articles, versus a corpus negative-to-positive ratio of **0.58 [c1]**. The topic’s ratio is **13.69 [c1]**, or **23.6 times the baseline [c1]**. This describes the tool’s article-level polarity classification, not the stance or quality of reporting.

Frequent labelled themes include politics (**226 articles [c1]**), technology (**141 [c1]**), government (**87 [c1]**), and elections (**82 [c1]**). Frequent subcategories include voter suppression allegations (**48 [c1]**) and election fraud investigations (**38 [c1]**). Counts can overlap; labels cover different subsets of the corpus.

Entity labels frequently include Meta (**46 articles [c1]**), Republican Party (**29 [c1]**), Joe Biden (**126 [c1]**), Elon Musk (**77 [c1]**), and Kamala Harris (**43 [c1]**). These are machine-assigned, unverified co-occurrences, not proof of involvement or prominence.

A central-match feed returned **five articles [c1]** despite a request for eight [c1]. One critical item was returned for the recent critical window, so this feed cannot support a comprehensive critical-headlines list. It includes an item dated 2026-04-15 [c1] from New Telegraph, “Ekiti Poll: EU Moves To Tackle Election Misinformation,” [linked article](https://newtelegraphng.com/ekiti-poll-eu-moves-to-tackle-election-misinformation/) [c1].

The publisher concentration estimate comes from only **16 sampled articles [c1]**, covering **15 distinct publishers [c1]**. Winnipeg Free Press led that sample with **12.5% [c1]**; the top three accounted for **24.9% [c1]**. This does not establish full-window source concentration.

## Trend

The monthly series shows sharp peaks in August and October 2024 [c1], then lower counts overall. The first and last thirds were **152 versus 17 articles [c1]**, a decline of **88.8% (calculated from [c1])**; this comparison excludes the censored newest boundary bucket under Prism’s growth method. May 2026’s one article [c1] is partial and should not be read as a completed-month collapse.


## Comparison

On the negative-to-positive ratio scale, topic coverage is **13.69 [c1]** versus **0.58 [c1]** for the corpus baseline: **23.6× [c1]** the baseline. The baseline is ordinary news coverage in Prism’s corpus; it is not a matched comparison group of election stories.

## Geography

Prism placed **181 of 235 matching articles [c1]** (**77.0% [c1]**) to a country. These are places articles are about, not where they were published. The United States led with **172 placed articles [c1]**; Colombia had **46 [c1]** and Georgia **17 [c1]**. The denominator is placed-eligible matches; ambiguous place resolution can misclassify articles, so the geography is indicative.

## Drill-down

Layer identifiers: `themes.categories`, `themes.subcategories`, `themes.tags`, `entities.organizations`, `entities.people`, `geography.country`, and `sources.publishers` [c1]. Counts and labels above inherit the matching and labelling caveats.

## Verdict
- Answer: In the news corpus, 236 articles mention "election misinformation" between 2024-06-01 and 2026-05-31 [c1]. 208 of them (88%) are critical [c1]. Volume peaked at 51 in October 2024 [c1] and has fallen to 1–3 a month in 2026 [c1]. About 52% of the articles with a place are about the United States [c1].
- Decision: Treat this as a thin, event-driven topic in this corpus. Do not use it as a general indicator of public attention.
- Confidence: medium - the counts come from one call under mention matching. Publisher concentration rests on a 16-article sample, and the volumes are small.
- What would change it: A central-match count or a wider publisher sample showing a very different volume or concentration.

## What the data shows
- Volume: 236 articles (mention match) from 2024-06-05 to 2026-05-01, within a window of 2024-06-01 to 2026-05-31 [c1]. 208 were critical [c1].
- Series: the monthly series is charted below. Peaks were 51 in 2024-10 and 44 in 2025-09 [c1]. Several months had zero articles [c1].
- Tone: 219 negative, 16 positive, 1 neutral [c1]. That is 92.8% negative [c1]. The negative-to-positive ratio is 13.69 against a corpus baseline of 0.58, a factor of 23.6 [c1].
- Themes (categories, share of labelled matches): politics 32.9%, technology 20.5%, government 12.7%, elections 11.9% [c1]. Leading subcategories were voter suppression allegations (48 articles) and election fraud investigations (38) [c1].
- Organisations: Meta 46 articles, the Republican Party 29, Facebook 15 [c1]. These are machine-assigned labels, not verified identities [c1].
- People: Joe Biden 126, Elon Musk 77, Kamala Harris 43, Mark Zuckerberg 33 [c1].
- Places: United States 172 articles (52.3%), Colombia 46 (14.0%), Georgia 17 (5.2%) [c1]. placed_pct is 77.0% (181 of 235 matched) [c1]. The place is where the article is about, not where it was published [c1]. Georgia may be the US state or the country, because the labels can collide [c1].
- Critical headlines found in the call (only 5 returned):
  - 2026-04-15, newtelegraphng.com, "Ekiti Poll: EU Moves To Tackle Election Misinformation", https://newtelegraphng.com/ekiti-poll-eu-moves-to-tackle-election-misinformation/ [c1]. Its polarity is positive, though it came back in the critical panel.
  - 2025-10-23, theconversation.com, a report that 60% of adults saw election misinformation before the 2025 Australian federal election [c1].
  - 2025-10-09, arstechnica.com, YouTube's "second chance" programme for banned creators [c1].
  - 2024-10-31, euronews.com, fact checks on X failing to counter US election misinformation [c1].
  - 2024-10-31, winnipegfreepress.com, the same report on crowd-sourced fact checks [c1].
- Source concentration: the top publisher has 12.5% and the top three 24.9% [c1]. The sample is only 16 articles across 15 publishers, so this is indicative only [c1].

## Trend
```prism-chart
{"id":"monthly","kind":"line","title":"Monthly articles mentioning election misinformation","unit":"articles","window":{"from":"2024-06-01","to":"2026-06-01"},"x":{"field":"period","type":"temporal"},"series":[{"name":"articles","source":"call:news.overview#1","points":[["2024-06",4],["2024-07",12],["2024-08",44],["2024-09",18],["2024-10",51],["2024-11",18],["2024-12",2],["2025-01",3],["2025-02",2],["2025-03",1],["2025-04",1],["2025-05",0],["2025-06",3],["2025-07",10],["2025-08",6],["2025-09",44],["2025-10",7],["2025-11",3],["2025-12",3],["2026-01",0],["2026-02",0],["2026-03",1],["2026-04",2],["2026-05",1]]}],"caption":"Coverage spiked around the 2024 US election and in September 2025, then fell to near zero.","supports":"Volume peaked at 51 in October 2024 and has fallen to 1–3 a month in 2026."}
```
- The early third of the window holds 152 articles and the late third 17 [c1]. That is a ratio of 0.11, and the tool labels the direction "falling" [c1].
- Critical articles fell from 129 to 17, a ratio of 0.13 [c1].
- The September 2025 spike (44 articles, all critical) is not explained by this call [c1].

## Comparison
- Baseline: the corpus-wide negative-to-positive ratio of 0.58 [c1].
- This topic's ratio is 13.69, which is 23.6 times the baseline [c1]. Its negative share is 92.8% [c1].
- Early versus late: the 152 articles in the early third are about 8.9 times the 17 in the late third (computed from [c1]).

## Geography
- The US accounts for 172 articles (52.3%) [c1]. Colombia has 46 (14.0%) with a lift of 28.8 [c1], and Georgia 17 [c1].
- Colombia's lift is high, but this call does not say why.
- Coverage of the places is 77.0% (placed_pct) [c1]. Labels after 2026-05-01 are not yet written, so recent months under-report places [c1].

## Method and limits
- Window: 2024-06-01 to 2026-05-31 (end exclusive 2026-06-01) [c1]. Today is 2026-10-23, so the data stops about 145 days short of today (computed). Nothing after May 2026 is covered, including the 2026 US midterms period.

- Cannot answer: how much of the coverage was fact-checking and how much was spreading the claims; audience size; counts for other languages or outlets outside the corpus; why the September 2025 spike happened.
- Interpretation: the fall after 2024 is consistent with the news cycle following the US election, but the call does not establish that cause.
- The theme labels include odd entries, such as employee benefits and metavision.com. Those are likely label noise and need article-level checks.

## References
